analysis.one_liner: Eliminates federal income tax on all interest and dividends received by individuals.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in February 1995 with seven cosponsors, never left the House Ways and Means Committee and died without a vote when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have struck dividends from domestic corporations and all interest income out of taxable income entirely, starting with tax year 1995. It spelled out detailed rules for mutual funds, real estate investment trusts, and trusts so their payouts would also qualify. It was referred to the tax-writing committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who receive dividend and interest income, which rises steeply with wealth — the top of the income distribution holds the large majority of taxable dividends and bond interest. Mutual funds, real estate investment trusts, banks, and other issuers of interest-bearing products would also gain, because tax-free returns make their products more attractive and let them pay lower rates.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes dividends from domestic corporations and all interest income from an individual's gross income, so none of it would be subject to federal income tax, effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 1994.

It writes pass-through mechanics so that distributions from regulated investment companies (mutual funds) and real estate investment trusts count as excludable dividends or interest, and so trust beneficiaries can claim the exclusion on amounts allocated to them.

It carves out only narrow exceptions: dividends from tax-exempt charities and farmers' cooperatives stay taxable, and nonresident aliens get the exclusion only for income connected to a U.S. business.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and with it every taxpayer who does not live on dividends and interest. Excluding this income from tax would create a large revenue gap that would have to be closed through spending cuts, higher taxes on wages, or more borrowing. Wage earners — who cannot convert their pay into untaxed dividends and interest — would bear a comparatively larger share of the remaining burden.

drawbacks.text: Because the exclusion applies to every dollar of dividends and interest with no income cap [S3], the largest dollar savings go to households with the largest investment portfolios, while the lost revenue must be made up by everyone else.
The bill contained no offsetting revenue provisions anywhere in its text, so it would have added to the deficit or forced other tax increases and spending cuts.

Backers would also have had to acknowledge the administrative shift: income that until now is reported on individual returns would move to a system of payer designations by funds and trusts, with 45-day written notices determining what shareholders may exclude.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was simple and would have ended a genuine double-taxation complaint — corporate profits are taxed at the entity level and again when paid out as dividends. But it was drafted as a blanket exclusion with no cap and no offset, so its benefits would have concentrated among the highest-income households while the cost was spread across everyone else through lost revenue. A narrower design aimed at small savers would have addressed the same complaint at a fraction of the cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Philip Crane of Illinois introduced the bill on February 24, 1995, joined by Reps. Blute, McKeon, and Hancock as original cosponsors.
Seven Republicans signed on as cosponsors in total.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction.

That referral is the last action ever taken: the bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion activity in the record, and it died at the end of the Congress on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the federal Treasury kept the revenue from taxing dividends and interest, and no new burden was shifted onto wage income. Investors with large portfolios, who would have been the main beneficiaries, gained nothing from the bill's failure to advance.

for.name: Rep. Philip M. Crane
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and issued introductory remarks on the day of introduction.

against.name: Rep. Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the committee took no action after the referral.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; the bill's only recorded support was the Republican sponsor and seven Republican cosponsors, with no Democratic cosponsors and no recorded opposition.

industries.note: Dividends and taxable interest are concentrated in the highest-income households, and the exclusion is uncapped, so the tax savings would be largest at the top. The lost revenue would be replaced by taxes or cuts borne broadly. [S3]

industries.industry: Mutual funds and real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The bill writes detailed rules so fund and REIT distributions qualify as excludable dividends or interest, making those products more attractive to investors. Savers holding the funds share the benefit. [S3]
Tax-free interest would raise demand for deposits and bonds, letting issuers pay lower rates. Savers gain from the exclusion, but issuers capture part of the benefit through cheaper funding.
